en: In this work,

a clear compendium is made of that very same non-apprehension which, according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), is scattered [throughout various texts] and resides in the nature of things. (1)
When negation is the probandum, non-apprehension is the third logical mark (*liṅga*).
And if that [non-apprehension] were merely the absence of apprehension, how could there be the cognition of anything?
Or [is it] the cause of practice; and how is there even the practice of that?
Therefore, like the case of "non-eatables" and so forth, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is simply the apprehension of something else by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
In that regard as well, if it were merely the apprehension of "the other," [then...]
In that case, upon the perception of any single thing, there would follow the undesirable consequence of negating everything.
If it is argued that the negation of identity with everything is indeed intended,
then the negation of its location [in all other things] is likewise unavoidable.
Thus, this is the distinction:
for when there is an object of cognition, the cognition of it may necessarily arise or it may not.
The wise hold that non-apprehension is our desired basis for the cognition of the absence of something else,
provided that when [the locus] is being perceived, there occurs the thought of that [other thing].
The negation of things remote by place, time,
or nature is necessarily [the result] of the deficiency of other conditions for perception;
by this, it is shown that the establishment of the cognition of non-existence belongs to that which has attained the status of being a "perceptible" (*dṛśya*) object.

Therefore, there is no consequence of negating everything. And when something is being cognized, that cognition which necessarily arises with respect to it is accepted as the [valid] knowledge of that very thing, and not of anything else.
"They are capable of projecting a continuous stream of the certainty of the non-existence of the second" means that by this it is stated that there is not merely an absence [of the second],
but rather, through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is a cognition of another specific thing.

And here, by the force of the phrase "of that very one alone," otherwise there would be no proof of non-existence, because the perception of another would remain unprohibited; for example: "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived despite being perceptible."
As in the phrase "somewhere something [is not perceived].

In that context, regarding the term "of the perceptible," one should understand that both its specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) and the completeness of other conditions for perception (*upalambhapratyayāntarasākalya*) have been stated.
Regarding the term "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*), the meaning is "the perception of the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*).
And that [locus] is either the ground which has attained the status of being the substratum for the counter-positive and the probans,
or something else not in contact with the cognition of a single sense-organ,
or yet another.
Because of the general statement that when something is being perceived, that which is to be negated must necessarily be apprehended; in that case,
if a portion of the earth is apprehended...
If the jar-born [Agastya] alone is to be established,
then he alone is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
what is the need for dependence on anything else?
But when [the cognition occurs] in the sky,
then too it is that very same thing designated as "light," or else it is something else, such as a jar.
[The object] has an indefinite duration.
However, in the case of the negation of a tangible [object], this very [negation] applies.
By this, [it is shown that] it is associated with a single cognition.
The counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) has been explained;
however, in some cases it is otherwise, as for example: "There is no taste here for one who swallows a lamp, because of the non-perception of a perceptible object."
Thus, touch alone is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). For when both [touch and color] exist, their cognition is not restricted to a single form, as is the case with a beverage (*pānaka*).
But then, how is it that even when only the visible form (*rūpa*) is seen from a distance?
Is there not a negation of taste? No, because for that which is spatially remote, there is an absence of the capacity for perception.
Because the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile senses function by reaching their objects, it has been said:
"When one thing is being perceived, that which is necessarily perceived [along with it] is indeed [the object].
Nor is there a negation of form (rūpa) during the experience of taste.
Even then, it is because that definition does not apply.
(2) Likewise, the negation of form is not established even by the non-perception of sound;
for in deep darkness, even though form exists, [it is not perceived].
Verbal cognition is not non-deviant from knowledge.
In the case of light, however, there is no negation of that which is actually being perceived; nor is there any fault in the negation of that which is unperceived yet capable of being perceived.
Because it does not abandon its characteristic of being tall.

By this, it is shown that when a temple or similar structure is perceived, the establishment of the absence of the sound of a drum or other such instruments in that location does not necessarily depend upon the cognition of another sound.
If it is argued that there is no rule for their simultaneous cognition,
this is not the case even for a portion of ground and a jar;
however, when both exist—
The absence of a rule regarding the cognition of a single form is equally applicable to perception in that case as well;

for there is no distinction whether a single cognition is invariably concomitant with the apprehension of another [object], or whether it is invariably concomitant with another cognition that apprehends that other object.
The same applies to other [cognitions] produced by a single sense-faculty;
for even in a pitch-black room, the absence of a lamp [is known] from another cognition— which lacks the form of that [lamp]— and ultimately even from conceptual construction,
if [it exists].
This is merely following the conventions of others.
In reality, however, it is only the actually existent darkness that can come into contact with a single cognition along with the lamp; so what is the use of anything else?

Now, even though there is a specific nature [in the object], the fitness for apprehension consists in the proximity of other conditions; and that, although it serves as the cause for cognitions produced by different sense organs, [is still required].
It is not employed for the determination of the cognition of distinct sensory objects;

therefore, when a negation is made regarding the doubt that another object might be present due to another cognition, this applies even ultimately to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that possesses a determinate form.
How could it be produced by that which is visible?
It is said:
Indeed, it is not dependent on the accomplishment of the proximity of other conditions.
It is indeed sensory cognition with respect to the same sense faculty;
however, it is also the perception of a particular state of the personal existence characterized by the five aggregates.
When no illuminator other than the specific nature of the sense organ itself is required— as is the case with sound, lamps, and so forth— [then the object is directly perceived].

For in that case, who can prevent the establishment of the non-existence of something by a cognition— whether from any source whatsoever— that lacks the respective forms [of that thing], provided that the person has previously heard of or seen it and knows the state and application of its sense-faculties?
What, then, is the utility of apprehending another cognition,
since the absence of that [first] cognition is established simply by the non-arising of a cognition of the awareness of that state?
Or how, from a sensory cognition whose object is distinct [from the object of the inference], can there be the negation of another?
To this it has been said:
"Non-existence has no capacity anywhere," and so forth. Therefore, another cognition is not relied upon to ascertain the excellence of the sense organ;
rather, it is for the purpose of generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). In that regard:
Just as a cognition associated with a common sense-organ is capable of determining the absence of another [object],

so too is any other [cognition] capable of doing so, provided it exists and lacks the form of a cognition of some other object that is invariably concomitant; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.
If it is asked how this is so:
here, desire and non-desire have no causal efficacy;
rather, [efficacy belongs] to those two whose positive and negative concomitance is followed [by the result].
It is the acceptance of the state of cause and effect.

Just as the cognition of a patch of ground, due to its restriction to a single form, follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) as replicated by the conceptual exclusion of other things,
so it is for one who casts a lamp into his mouth.
The cognition of that [taste] occurs through the cognition of the absence of taste, due to the restriction to the mere form of touch;
for there is no distinction between intervention and non-intervention in the arising of these two.

Likewise, for one whose nose is applied to pure water and who neither touches nor sees it, even though there is no direct experience of another odor, there occurs a conceptual construction (vikalpa) through the cognition of the absence of odor; this [cognition] is devoid of the form [of that absence].
(4) If it is argued that this is inferential (laiṅgika), we say no.
Because there is no intervention for one who has reached the stage of cultivation,
that which is certain at the very moment of its apprehension is not inferential.
Or it is established by direct perception,
as in "blue is not yellow," and this is the case when [the object] is present.
For one who possesses a conceptualization of the mere form of directing the nose toward milk, there is the certainty that "there is no odor. In this case,

if the experience of a conceptualization of a restricted form were not the cause for establishing the mere absence of the cognition of odor, then let there likewise be no experience of blue for the cognition of the absence of yellow.

Or rather, for one who maintains that there is direct perception of a person here [in this world], it is difficult to avoid the same [conclusion] regarding the other world as well. And that very same perception is called "non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi) with respect to the object to be negated for a particular individual,
just as has been stated.

And that [inference] is a logical mark (*liṅga*) which, with respect to a deluded cognizer, determines the absence in a particular substratum (*dharmiviśeṣa*) according to a prior convention; however, for one who is not deluded and lacks the absence of repeated practice,
this determination is indeed stable, being free from any subsequent doubt.
It is said to be "initiated by perception.
Now, is it not the case that no linguistic convention regarding non-existence is produced by perception?
Nor has it been stated that perception is fruitful by way of determining the non-existence of an object.
Rather, it is by means of the very ascertainment of the absence of cognition that it includes the ascertainment of the absence of the object; thus, it is said to be produced by perception. And that—
Even that which arises immediately after the capacity [of a cause] is, when overcome by doubt, inferential with respect to a deluded person.

For there is no restriction on an object to having the nature of illumination as there is for cognition; since its existence is not contradicted even if it is unperceived, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the refuge.
But for one who is not deluded, there is the non-perception of the pervader,
because the existence of a perceptible object is pervaded by its being an object of perception; this is due to the inability to distinguish between these two.
Some say that the former [the self] is deluded;
that is incorrect, for just as knowledge is not non-luminous...
Since it is likewise impermanent and invisible even externally,
just like that [object], its absence cannot be precluded by perception, and thus the conventional usage of "absence" remains unobstructed.
Knowledge is perceptible by its very nature alone,

whereas external objects are perceived only in some cases, in some ways, and at some times. In that regard, for a cognizer possessing a particular degree of practice, there arises— through mere perception— cognition even of an external particular, just as there is of the generality of another cognition.
How can this instantaneous establishment of negation, which is repeatedly experienced, be denied?
If it is argued that this is because inference regarding reality is possible,
[we reply that] even the ascertainment of the intended fitness is not produced by perception.
This is of little consequence.
Furthermore, the aforementioned doubt does not arise solely by virtue of external objects;
rather, this perception consists of a vision whose nature is free from conceptual construction (*asaṃsṛṣṭavikalpa*).

Otherwise, if there were perception of a conceptualization whose nature is that which is perceived, then the non-perception [of other objects] would strike down the conceptual construction within sensory cognition; this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that such things could not be expressed.
Therefore, even in the case of a cognition, there may at times be a reflective awareness (vimarśa) of another cognition.

Even regarding an object, certainty is a state of mind in which no internal doubt remains; thus, the establishment of the capacity of perception or anything else occurs through a division of its states,
and not through a division of its genus.

If it is argued that by the statement beginning with "nanv ekopalambhānubhavāt," the capacity [of the argument] has been stated precisely as the negation of another cognition, and that experience is likewise [of this nature], we say no; for, as follows: (6)
"This is not perceived" is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
likewise, for one who has practiced [the meditation], "this does not exist" also arises instantaneously.
However, for one who has not practiced, the certainty is simply the absence of cognition.
However, since there is an absence of the object by way of that [cognition], the treatise expresses it in such a manner with reference to that.
In the same way, effort and so forth, which are associated with a single cognition, are also to be explained.
For this very reason, it is said that those of great intelligence determine all aspects from the very first moment of perception;
and with respect to those of duller intelligence, effort is required at various stages.
Therefore, for those of sharp intellect,
just as in the case of distinguishing a gem from silver, even the conventional usage of its negation is unavoidable based on perception alone.
Furthermore, non-existence (abhāva) does not possess a physical form.
It is not by means of a form that excludes others which must be directly perceived,
but rather that which is to be engaged with in linguistic usage;
and that [engagement] occurs through a sharp [cognition] due to the restriction to a single form.
It is indeed possible for the perceiver to act [upon this].
However, one who is dull-witted may still doubt even when there has been an initial ascertainment of non-existence.
He proceeds with that conventional usage by following the mere non-perception of the perceptible;
however, one who is less proficient than even that [first type], even when there is non-perception of the perceptible—

One who is in doubt proceeds by means of the non-perception of the pervader; however, for one who is not deluded, there is no proceeding by this [means], for it is precisely when perception lacks clarity that inference is sought.
And that proficiency is established through the generation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
as well as its state of being more intense,
because in that [latter] case there is an absence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). (7)
However, the operation of negation by means of perception has been demonstrated specifically against the Cārvāka, who indeed accepts the non-existence of things as distinct [from cognition],
because of the reasoning that [perception] depends upon the causal capacity of the object.
Furthermore, the determination of apprehension for perception, unlike inference, does not depend on certainty,
but rather on appearance.
And its very possession of a determinate form is precisely the manifestation of the non-existence of anything other than that;
therefore, the capacity of perception to function as a conventional designation for absence is unavoidable.
But the negation [of inference] everywhere is based on non-perception; this, however, is not a rejection of perception, but rather of other types of inferential marks (*liṅga*).
Just as it is said that there are only two means of establishing a positive injunction,
so too this negation of odor in water is established by perception itself, because there is no interval [of inference], and not through inference.
Furthermore, what here is the mark (*liṅga*) that is non-deviant from the absence of odor?
If it is argued that it is the non-perception of the effect, which is cognition, then [we reply:
when the cognition that perceives itself is the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
This is also logical:
when that [object] is indeed perceived through direct perception, then there is the cessation of that which is suitable for direct perception.
If it were not so, then even the non-perception of a visible object, such as a jar, would not occur;
thus,
this [position] is merely the fruit of deceiving oneself regarding the nature of the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
And if this proponent says this without having ascertained the excellence of the sense faculty, then even though the odor and so forth are present, [they would not be perceived].
It follows that [the object] is not perceived.
Now, one who is certain should see that this is sufficient by means of the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, when a cause or the like is merely suspected to exist beyond the range of perception (*parokṣa*), he applies the non-perception of the effect with effort. At present—
Furthermore, it is incoherent to suggest that one would doubt even what is established by direct perception out of fear of some slight defect.
Therefore, this is established:
when one thing is being perceived, that which is necessarily perceived as well— being apprehended by the same sense organ— is not distinct from it.
Alternatively, non-apprehension is the cognition of that which is not graspable by the senses;
and that [non-apprehension] establishes only conventional usage,
since otherwise it would be established by perception.
And for that purpose,
it was stated that [the locus] is the support for the stability of the persistence of the cognition of separation,
but not for the certainty of separation.

And just as for two things that are necessarily perceived together, one cognition serves to negate the other, so it is also for two things that are necessarily not perceived together; thus he says, "or not.
For the meaning is: where, with respect to the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the cognition of the other would not necessarily occur.

Just as in the case of "this is blue, it is not non-blue," here too, it is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is to be established. By this, contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇa-virodha*) is explained.

But is this not already established by the principle that when something is being perceived, it is possible for a cognition of whatever else is invariably associated with it to arise? For even that which is invisible is negated as being identical [with the perceived object] precisely by virtue of its being treated as visible.
If it is argued: "Only that which is already conceived is negated;
otherwise, since the distinction [between the seen and the unseen] is admitted by its very nature, what is the purpose of this separate statement?"
In that case, this absence characterized as destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-lakṣaṇa*) is explained as "or rather, it would not exist.
The meaning is: even when [the cognition] has arisen, the mind necessarily ceases with respect to that object of knowledge (*vedya*) which [is present].
Furthermore, when there is sublation of existence, non-existence alone is logical as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), as in the case:
"There is no cold here because of fire. By this, the opposition characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is explained. (9)

If it is argued that "in darkness there is necessarily non-perception, and thus there is no necessary apprehension of a contradictory [property]," we reply: no, this is not with respect to a single cognizer.
This is a general characteristic; however,
there is indeed the perception of form even in the absence of light by certain individuals.
Or rather, it may be possible [to prevent death] by means of specific medicinal ointments and the like;
however, in the case of the destruction of the life-force (*sattva*), there is indeed a fixed rule, so there is no fault.
But surely, even in this case, if it were cold...
How is there a distinction from the previous case, given that the cognition of fire is restricted to a single form?
It is not so, because the negation [of such restriction] is intended only in the case of what is accessible through touch. If that is so, then...

Even though the cognition of cold has arisen, it is impossible to ascertain that it has ceased upon the perception of fire, because this [cessation] is not perceived at another time; for it is the perception [of the cessation] occurring at that specific time which is intended. If that is so, then [the inference] would have its operation obstructed by the recollection of the previously apprehended contradiction.

The determination of non-existence cannot arise merely from the operation of perception; let it not be so! However, even when there is an obstruction, it is precisely that cognition which is incompatible [with the object's presence] that serves as the factor for determining non-existence, and not the mere absence of any other [cognition]. Thus, there is no damage to the foundation of the established principle of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
And it is not accepted here either that this is established merely for the sake of conventional usage;
thus he says: "But since the subsequent [cognition] is dependent upon memory, therefore even non-existence is to be proven here. And when that is established...

The meaning is that even conventional usage, which is characterized by the stability of that certainty, is not merely that [certainty] itself. Likewise, when there is a denial of the reason or the pervader, non-existence (*abhāva*) also functions as the probandum (*sādhya*), as in: "There is no smoke here, because of the absence of fire."

"There is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees. For in this case, the mere perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)— namely, fire and tree— is not independent of the recollection of the previously established knowledge of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).
It produces the ascertainment of the absence of smoke and the *aśiṃśapā* tree; therefore, here too, the establishment of the conventional usage of proving non-existence occurs.
These, then, are the reasons for negation: the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

[The two types of non-apprehension are] non-apprehension of the cause and non-apprehension of the pervader; likewise, there are two [types] that establish by way of affirmation. Thus, five reasons would result. No, [it is not so].
Because non-apprehension is one, being based on the commonality of non-apprehension; moreover, non-apprehension is of itself and of another,
[namely] of the cause and the pervader.
The non-perception of another effect or of another pervaded [property] is itself called the non-perception of another cause or the non-perception of another pervader;
for indeed, the direct perception of one thing is precisely the non-perception of another.

Likewise, for someone, the non-perception of the essential nature itself is called the non-perception of the cause or the pervader with respect to the effect or the pervaded; thus, there is no difference in the reality of the thing due to a difference in designation.

Therefore, since the negation of everything results precisely from the non-perception of its own-nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), there are only three types of logical mark (*liṅga*). By this, it should be understood that the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) implies the non-perception of the cause when that cause is capable [of producing the effect].
Or, it is because of the explanation of the word "cause" (*hetu*) as having the meaning of a logical mark (*liṅga*), as for example:
"There are no causes of smoke here whose capacity is unobstructed, because of the absence of smoke. (11)
How, then, is the statement "there is no touch of frost here because of fire" included within the category of perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*)?
In this case as well, there is a non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of itself and another [non-perception].
For when there is a non-apprehension of the nature [of cold]— which consists in the apprehension of fire, the contradictory of the pervader (vyāpaka)—
this is called the "apprehension of that which is contradictory to the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) with respect to the pervaded (vyāpya), namely the touch of frost; thus, there is no fault.
And although that [non-cognition] could also be described as the non-apprehension of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), nevertheless,
it is designated as such for the purpose of demonstrating its nature as the cognition of a contradictory counter-correlate (*viruddhapratiyogipratīti*).
In this manner, the perception of the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) and other such reasons are to be explained.
In all cases, it is non-existence alone that is to be proven, because [the object] is not established by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*).
"But the conventional usage [of 'non-perception'] is mediated by that.
Now, one might ask: "In cases such as the perception of the incompatible (*viruddhopalabdhi*), how can there be the conventional usage of non-perception? To this it has been said:
Non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
And the counter-positive is of two kinds. Among these, when the counter-positive is contradictory (*viruddha*),...
Then, the employment of a contradictory term establishes that the word "perception" (upalabdhi) must be used in this manner;
for when the remaining counter-positive (pratiyogin) is understood, [the contradiction is evident].

When the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) or the word "perceptible" (*dṛśya*) is employed, it is designated by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with reference to that which is to be negated.
Thus, in one case [the presence of] apprehensibility is understood, while in the other, non-apprehensibility is understood. But as for its true nature:
There is no fault in saying "only one";

and when the contradictory counter-correlate is such that the negation of a second [entity] is necessarily beyond perception (*parokṣa*), then for that [second entity] as well, it is not necessarily [the case].
Non-apprehension is indeed perception,
but it is also inference;
for that which is contradictory removes the existence of another by its own existence.
The counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is considered [to be present].
And who can prevent that which, even if remote, becomes such [a counter-correlate]?
However, when the counter-correlate is necessarily perceived simultaneously, it must be one that is indeed capable of being perceived.
Regarding negation, there is necessarily a dependence upon perception;
for if a jar were present in a location that is being inferred,
it would certainly be perceived— such is the logical capacity [of the inference], since inference is not applicable where perception is possible.
Since there is no rule regarding the commencement [of an action], how can there be a negation?
If it is argued that, in this case, there is no negation because it is merely a conceptual construction (vikalpa), we say: no.

Even in that case, when the form of conceptual construction is being experienced, it is said that the desired external object would also be experienced through the efficacy of the sense faculty provided there is no impairment; however, this does not apply to the object of conceptualization itself.

If an external object were being conceptualized, it would be possible for a second [object] also to be cognized. Even when an external object is being conceptualized, why should it not be the case that another [object] located in that same place is indeed perceived?

For the cognition of a counter-positive is not the basis for the superimposition of visibility upon another thing; rather, it is the cause for the production of the ascertainment of non-existence, because [the counter-positive] is an existent reality.
And since that [non-apprehension] belongs to conceptual construction as well, what is the distinction?
If it is argued that there must be conformity with the cognizer, then it would be correct to maintain conformity even for those things associated within a single cognition.

This is not so; for even when only a remnant of odor in water or of taste in fire is perceived, we observe that there is merely a conventional designation of their absence. Furthermore, if you maintain that non-perception consists in the non-perception of the effect of cognition (*jñāna*), then since that same principle applies elsewhere as well, what is the point of [specifying] "that which is associated with the same cognition"?
If it is argued that only a capable entity is negated through the non-perception of its effect,

then it follows that even though fragrance and so forth exist in water and the like, they are not perceived due to a defect in the sense organs; thus, the fruit of your great labor on the treatise is truly immense!
For he, even when no cause for defect is perceived,
entertains doubt by imagining that [the object] might be obscured by something powerful and so forth; however,
on the ground, there is no non-perception caused by such [obscuration].
Even when there is acuity of the sense faculties, why does one not doubt while anticipating [an error]?
Therefore, during the stage of practice, worldly transaction proceeds precisely through the persistence of that same state. (13)
But for the Lord of Logic (Nyāyanātha), there is neither questioning nor relinquishing in accordance with worldly convention;
rather, even regarding this much...

This is stated by way of bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*) to demonstrate that there is no impairment of our own definition [of omniscience] even when it is established that all minds are non-omniscient;
just as, for instance, even though all minds are determined to be non-omniscient, that very person is indeed omniscient.

Furthermore, in common practice, it is observed that the ascertainment of absence occurs even with respect to another counter-positive, just as it does for one who perceives something associated within a single cognition; since this is both common and non-contradictory, the apprehension of what is associated within a single cognition is not a necessary requirement.
Moreover, in the state of relying upon conceptual construction, it is logical that the mere awareness of its own form is the means for establishing the negation of others.
In the same way, because the capacity for direct perception is observed through repeated practice,
the apprehension of even a remote contradictory [object],
which consists of inference, establishes the absence of its opposite.

Just as "there is no cold here because of smoke," so too should the perception of the effect of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) be understood, for example: "there is no frost here because of smoke."
This is the explanation for the time of formal application (prayoga), having combined these points;
however, in reality, "cold is not fire" is a single formal application.

To avoid the charge of that being unestablished, another [proponent] states: "And there is fire here because of smoke," and likewise, "there is no frost because of fire. For that which is contradictory to the pervader is indeed contradictory.
"And fire [is inferred] from smoke. The remainder should also be inferred in this manner:
if there is a non-perception of the nature of the cause and so forth, it is the non-perception of another's cause and so forth.
It is of the nature of a relative negation (paryudāsa).
How then [is it applied] to things that lack any designation (nirupākhya)?
For example, "the son of a barren woman is not a speaker" because of the absence of consciousness.
Thus, even in that case, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) consists in the cognition of the mental image itself as being devoid of consciousness;
and the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*) consists in the cognition [of it] through the exclusion of speakerhood. (14)

Furthermore, since all non-apprehensions (anupalabdhi) ultimately resolve into the reason of essential nature (svabhāvahetu), there is no fault in their being taught separately from the [other] means of establishing negation, because they involve a distinct determination.
Nevertheless, according to the sequence already stated, they function directly.

If it is asked: "How is it that the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anupalabdhi*) is made figurative by the venerable Master through a traditional designation as 'negation'? [The answer is:
if it is indeed the non-perception of the object to be negated that is perceived...
The negator intended there is figurative;
however, if it applies to the other [the opponent] as well, then it is primary—so what contradiction is there? Only this much.
One might ask: what is the purpose of speaking figuratively?
Even in that case, it is so that the negation may apply only to that which is perceptible, and not to anything else.
The inclusion [of the omniscient being, the dispassionate one, and so forth] therein is by way of their effects, namely, that they serve as the primary goals of human endeavor.
In reality, however, it is the non-perception of such a being—whether that being or anything else—as previously described, which serves as the proof. Thus ends the *Anupalabdhira-hasya*.
